title: Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee – Enhancing quality in employment and working conditions by introducing and promoting related tools (including AI) and strengthening social dialogue and collective bargaining (exploratory opinion requested by the Cypriot presidency)
text:
Official Journal of the European Union
EN
C series
C/2026/3220
2.7.2026
Opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee
Enhancing quality in employment and working conditions by introducing and promoting related tools (including AI) and strengthening social dialogue and collective bargaining
(exploratory opinion requested by the Cypriot presidency)
(C/2026/3220)
Rapporteur :
Nicoletta MERLO
Advisors
Emanuele DAGNINO (for the rapporteur)
Isaline OSSIEUR (for the Group I rapporteur)
Referral
Letter of 14/10/205 by the Cyprus Presidency of the Council of the EU
Legal basis
Article 304 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Exploratory opinion
Section responsible
Employment, Social Affairs and Citizenship
Adopted in section
24.2.2026
Adopted at plenary session
18.3.2026
Plenary session No
604
Outcome of vote
(for/against/abstentions)
157/77/10
1. Conclusions and recommendations
1.1.
The EESC underlines that artificial intelligence (AI) and algorithmic management (AM) can improve the quality of employment and working conditions if they respect the human-in-control principle, while also supporting economically, environmentally and socially sustainable growth by enhancing productivity and competitiveness in Europe.
1.2.
The Committee recognises the potential of AI as a strategic lever to strengthen occupational safety and health, notably through active risk prevention, early hazard detection and the automation of the most dangerous, strenuous or repetitive tasks, provided that risks of discrimination or misuse are prevented.
1.3.
The EESC highlights that the use of AI can enhance work organisation and work-life balance, bearing in mind that adequate organisational capacities, especially in SMEs, are essential for its effective adoption.
1.4.
The Committee acknowledges the contribution of AI and labour market intelligence tools in anticipating skills needs and supporting training, reskilling and professional development pathways, helping to reduce skills mismatches and increase workers’ employability.
1.5.
The EESC draws attention to the risks associated with the introduction of AI and AM, in particular in terms of work intensification, increased psychosocial risks, reduced decision-making autonomy and technostress. In line with the OSH framework, which requires employers to assess all risks to workers’ health and safety, these risks fall within the scope of the OSH risk assessment where relevant and should be addressed through appropriate measures, with the involvement of social partners and through collective bargaining at the appropriate level.
1.6.
In order to avoid opacity in algorithmic systems and the risk of discriminatory practices, the EESC underlines the importance of ensuring transparency, explainability and fairness in the use of AI and AM systems. These contribute to increasing trust in these technologies, and their legitimacy and social acceptance, especially among vulnerable groups.
1.7.
In order to prevent power asymmetries linked to the intensive use of data and workplace surveillance and monitoring practices, the EESC underlines the pivotal importance of promoting transparent, proportionate and adequately safeguarded data use, including clear limits on the use of intrusive applications.
1.8.
The EESC supports the European Parliament resolution ( 1 ) calling on the Commission to carry out a thorough assessment of existing legislation related to the deployment of AI and AM tools in the workplace and, on the basis of its results, to present an EU proposal specifically dedicated to AM at work to fully address the specificities of its impact on working conditions, while avoiding the creation of overlapping legal instruments and improving harmonisation of the internal market.
1.9.
The Committee acknowledges that currently applicable provisions, including those deriving from the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) ( 2 ) and the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) ( 3 ) should be fully implemented and enforced as regards the introduction of AI and AM tools in the workplace, while at the same time recognising that this presents an opportunity to extend to all workers the principles of the Platform Work Directive ( 4 ) on AM in order to strengthen their protections.
1.10.
The EESC underlines the central role of social dialogue and collective bargaining at all levels, as well as structured cooperation between the EU AI Office, the European Commission and the social partners, in ensuring that the deployment of AI contributes to a fair, inclusive and competitive digital transition, systematically taking into account the dimensions of gender, generations and vulnerability as well as the needs of SMEs.
2. General comments
2.1.
The EESC welcomes the request from the Cypriot Presidency to draw up an exploratory opinion on improving the quality of employment and working conditions through the introduction and promotion of appropriate tools, including artificial intelligence (AI), and on strengthening social dialogue and collective bargaining. In this regard, the Committee draws attention to the positions outlined in its 2025 opinion on Pro-worker AI: levers for harnessing the potential and mitigating the risks of AI in connection with employment and labour market policies ( 5 )
and its recently-adopted opinion on the Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council – Apply AI Strategy ( 6 )
.
2.2.
The EESC notes that AI ( 7 ) and/or algorithmic management (AM) practices ( 8 ) are now one of the main factors transforming EU democratic systems, societies and economies, including the labour market. However, their impact on work organisation and industrial relations is neither neutral nor predetermined, depending to a decisive extent on the political, regulatory and organisational choices that accompany the design, implementation and use of these technologies in business contexts and public services.
2.3.
The EESC also highlights the strategic challenges facing the EU as regards benefitting from AI, which is characterised by significant market imbalances and a high concentration of funding and technological development in the hands of non-European operators. As the effective implementation of AI systems could improve working conditions and create numerous high-quality jobs in the EU, this competitiveness gap is detrimental not only to European employers but also to European workers. In order to strengthen EU competitiveness and ensure technological sovereignty, it is essential to remove existing barriers, including but not limited to infrastructure limitations and the persistent skills shortage in the labour market ( 9 ) .
2.4.
The Committee stresses that the success of adopting AI cannot be assessed solely in technological terms. They are closely linked to complementary changes in work organisation, human resource management and business practices and require the proper implementation of the human-in-control principle. Competitiveness, productivity, the creation of quality jobs and improvements in working conditions are mutually reinforcing and should not be pursued independently of one another. To fully unlock the potential benefits that AI tools can have for efficiency, productivity and quality of work, businesses may need to adjust their internal processes, decision-making models and existing ways of involving workers.
2.5.
The Committee also draws attention to the current EU regulatory framework: the existing social and employment legislation and the social acquis already include provisions and safeguards which ensure that when AI and AM tools are deployed in the workplace, on the one hand the safe and fair working conditions of employees are safeguarded and on the other hand workers are involved in the deployment process of an AI tool. As stated by the Commission ( 10 ) , both the AI Act and the GDPR already establish comprehensive horizontal frameworks, while not precluding the Union or Member States from maintaining or introducing rules which are more favourable to workers in terms of protecting their rights in respect of the use of AI systems by employers ( 11 ) . Against this backdrop, the EESC nevertheless notes that the implementation and enforcement of the existing legal framework need to be monitored and further reinforced to fully ensure effective and fair deployment of AI tools in the workplace, so that AI can be both a driver for economic and technological progress and a vehicle for improving quality jobs in the EU.
2.6.
The EESC acknowledges the Commission’s specific commitment in the first-stage social partner consultation document for the Quality Jobs Act to consider, if necessary: 1) targeted complementary measures to strengthen workers’ protection and promote enhanced social dialogue; 2) possible simplification in the field of AI at work, reducing the burden on workers and companies; and 3) clarification on interaction with other EU rules such as on data protection, AI systems, information and consultation, or trade secrets. In the context of the world of work, regulatory simplification should go hand in hand with ensuring the enforcement and promotion of a high level of protection of fundamental rights and working conditions.
2.7.
To this end, the EESC, in line with its opinion Assessment of the Letta and Draghi reports on the functioning and competitiveness of the EU ’ s Single Market ( 12 ) , welcomes the recent European Parliament resolution on the use of AI and AM systems in the workplace ( 13 ) , which, underlining that regulatory responses at EU level should be carefully considered and preceded by an analysis of existing legislation, calls on the Commission to carry out an impact assessment complemented by a competitiveness and SME test and on the basis of this submit a proposal on AM in the workplace, which would address the remaining gaps in the protection of workers’ rights in existing legislation, avoiding creation of overlapping legal instruments and improving harmonisation of the internal market. Among the expected gaps and the aspects that would benefit from greater regulatory clarity, the EESC singles out those relating to workers’ involvement, effective human oversight and review of decisions, power imbalances and the prevention of psychosocial risks and intrusive practices. In the same vein, it is essential to ensure that simplification initiatives, such as the Digital Omnibus ( 14 ) , aimed at facilitating compliance and improving the consistency of the applicable rules, do not undermine the protection of fundamental rights and working conditions.
2.8.
The gender dimension, which is closely intertwined with the generational dimension, plays a particular role. On the one hand, many of the occupations most exposed to the impact of AI, such as clerical work and knowledge professions, have a strong female presence and a significant proportion of mature workers. On the other hand, AI and AM tools are used across sectors. The banking and manufacturing sectors are currently among the leading sectors and they are primarily male-dominated. These dynamics may disproportionately affect workers in more vulnerable situations, including persons with disabilities ( 15 ) , who often face additional barriers in accessing, adapting to and benefiting from digital technologies. Simultaneously, digital flexibility can help workers with care responsibilities, older workers, and persons with disabilities access the labour market ( 16 ) . The Committee therefore stresses the need to systematically integrate gender and generational perspectives, together with disability and vulnerability considerations, into AI governance and digital transition, in order to ensure that innovation contributes to increased productivity and an overall improvement in the quality of work throughout life. In this perspective, it is also in the common interest of all parties involved to promote effective training and retraining pathways that enable workers to acquire skills relevant in labour, with particular focus on accessibility and inclusiveness, as this promotes an inclusive and sustainable digital transition that improves competitiveness and productivity.
3. Specific comments
3.1. Tools for improving work quality
3.1.1.
The EESC recognises that the implementation of AI and other digital systems must be focused on improving both the competitiveness of the EU economy on the global market and the quality of jobs, with a sustainable improvement in working conditions. Especially if implemented through social dialogue at the appropriate level and with adequate involvement from workers’ representatives, which ensures that its use is consistent with social, organisational and employment sustainability, the adoption of AI can be a tool for increasing both productivity and job quality.
Health and safety at work and working conditions
3.1.2.
The integration of AI and AM into workplaces is a strategic lever for achieving the EU’s ‘zero deaths’ goal ( 17 ) , acting as an advanced tool for active prevention and risk monitoring. AI systems can contribute significantly to the early detection of hazards, the customisation of protective measures and the automation of dangerous, strenuous or repetitive tasks, significantly improving the effectiveness and efficiency of occupational safety interventions. Technologies such as proactive detection systems, smart PPE (Personal Protective Equipment) and algorithms for monitoring emergency situations can strengthen companies’ preventive capabilities, while using AI to increase the efficiency of inspections can improve the effectiveness of regulatory enforcement, provided that it is designed in such a way as to prevent risks of discrimination, unfair application or possible malfunctions.
3.1.3.
At the same time, the EESC draws attention to the psychosocial risks that can be associated with the introduction of AM and the intensification of work. In line with the OSH framework, which requires employers to assess all risks to workers’ health and safety, where relevant, phenomena such as increased workload, reduced decision-making autonomy, continuous physical and mental pressure resulting from AM and technostress fall within the scope of the OSH risk assessment and should therefore be addressed through specific measures, which should be identified with the involvement of workers’ representatives or through collective bargaining. These assessments and measures should also, where relevant, adopt a gender-sensitive approach and address all forms of violence and harassment at work, including cyber violence. The EESC will closely follow the work of EU-OSHA and Eurofound in this domain in order to complement analyses and data collection.
3.1.4.
The EESC welcomes the Commission’s commitment ( 18 ) to ‘review the Workplace Directive ( 19 ) and the Display Screen Equipment Directive ( 20 ) in consultation with the social partners’. This revision is a crucial step towards ‘updating OSH protection for modern workplaces, including telework, and in digital tools’ and is particularly vital for ‘better addressing psychosocial and ergonomic risks’.
Work organisation and work-life balance
3.1.5.
Pursuing greater productivity and organisational efficiency with the help of AI should lead to better overall conditions of workers, so that the adoption of new technologies simultaneously promotes efficiency and quality of work. This can be achieved by adequately taking into account the needs and perspectives of workers in the processes of introducing and using AI, through effective involvement of workers’ representatives and unions (through information and consultation mechanisms such as those provided by the Information and Consultation Directive ( 21 ) ).
3.1.6.
AI can promote a better work-life balance by increasing the flexibility of work organisation in terms of time and space and increasing workers’ ability to plan their activities ( 22 ) . However, the introduction of AI tools can involve significant organisational challenges for employers, depending on factors inherent to the company such as their size, business models and sector, as well as factors related to the AI tool. Addressing these organisational challenges through targeted capacity-building can enable AI to support innovation that delivers both productivity gains and improvements in the quality of work.
3.2. Tools and potential for identifying training and professional development needs
3.2.1.
AI can play an important role in anticipating professional and skills needs through labour market analysis tools, attributable to so-called labour market intelligence (LMI). Appropriate use of these tools can help improve understanding of the changes taking place and support the adaptation of training provision, reducing the mismatch between the skills required and those available and identifying the segments of the working population most at risk of not having the required skills. In addition, AI can support employment services in improving the matching of labour supply and demand, assisting candidates and workers in building targeted career paths, for example by suggesting training courses or retraining opportunities. However, such applications must be properly designed and verified to ensure fairness, reliability, inclusiveness and transparency.
3.2.2.
Alongside technical and specialist skills, basic digital skills are of central importance, as are transversal and relational skills, including the ability to solve complex problems and social skills. These skills are essential to enable workers to adapt to rapidly changing professional contexts and to interact knowledgeably with increasingly widespread technological systems. Investing in workers’ competencies and creativity will boost productivity and efficiency to the benefit of businesses.
3.2.3.
The EESC also highlights that particular attention should be paid to the most exposed or vulnerable workers (see above). In this context, training and lifelong learning are a key tool for investment, protection and inclusion. The Committee underlines that training is key to support workers in job transformations. Once again, the social partners should play a key role, given their knowledge of companies, sectors and local requirements. In order to raise awareness and improve critical thinking skills in relation to these tools the EESC welcomes the specific reference in Article 4 of the AI Act to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy.
3.3. Transparency and fairness of AI tools and AM
3.3.1.
The increasing application of AM in the field of work may give raise to considerations of transparency, fairness and the protection of fundamental rights. Such systems often rely on extensive forms of data collection and analysis and introduce new control dynamics of oversight that can influence labour relations and organisational decision-making. Ensuring the application of adequate safeguards and clear communication can help balance efficiency gains with the protection of workers’ interests.
A.
Data use, surveillance and power asymmetry
3.3.2.
AM systems involve the collection and processing of a variety of data, which may include biometric or behavioural information, sometimes applied across different purposes. To foster trust and maintain confidence, it is important to ensure that such data use is transparent, proportionate, and subject to adequate safeguards, helping to prevent unintended or undisclosed applications.
B.
System opacity, risk of algorithmic bias and discrimination
3.3.3.
Many AI systems and AM practices can be highly opaque, making it difficult to understand the criteria underlying automated or semi-automated decisions. By ensuring transparency, workers will acquire the ability to challenge decisions that significantly affect their professional status.
3.3.4.
There is also a risk that AI and AM can amplify bias and distortion present in historical data, contributing to the perpetuation of social inequalities and discriminatory practices, for example in staff selection or performance appraisal processes. The EESC notes that discriminatory decisions generated by automated systems may be perceived as more objective and thus less problematic from an ethical point of view than those taken by humans, with the risk of normalising unfair practices. On the other hand, the Committee underlines the possible role of AI – developed in a transparent manner and adequately supervised – as a useful tool for identifying and reducing the risks of discrimination and prejudice, especially against vulnerable groups, which are already present in people’s decision-making processes, offering the opportunity to promote greater equity in organisational practices.
C.
Safeguards and transparency to protect workers’ interests
3.3.5.
The EESC underlines that workers should be informed and consulted. In particular, the Committee emphasises the right of workers and their representatives to receive accessible, timely, clear and understandable information on the AI systems used or planned, prior to any implementation or substantial modification ( 23 ) .
3.3.6.
The Committee acknowledges that the introduction of AM systems should be preceded by a mandatory algorithmic impact assessment, including an analysis of the effects on fundamental rights and equality ( 24 ) . This assessment should be carried out with the full involvement of workers' representatives before the systems are launched ( 25 ) .
3.3.7.
The EESC stresses the importance of ensuring the effective implementation of the principle of human-in-control over automated decision-making processes, to ensure workers’ right to human supervision and to request a human review of decisions that have a significant impact on their working situation ( 26 ) .
3.3.8.
The Committee acknowledges the importance of clear limits on the use of intrusive applications in the workplace, such as monitoring of emotional data or non-work-related information ( 27 ) .
3.3.9.
In order to strengthen the protections already guaranteed by horizontal legislation with regard to the specific characteristics of the world of work, the EESC supports the extension of the principles relating to AM contained in the Platform Work Directive, with the necessary adjustments.
3.4. Role of enterprises, with particular emphasis on micro-enterprises and SMEs, social dialogue and collective bargaining
3.4.1.
The potential benefits of AI, including its contribution to reducing the productivity gap, can only be fully realised through consistent investment in innovation, infrastructure and human capital.
A.
Competitiveness and investment
3.4.2.
The effective adoption of AI technologies can require stronger managerial skills and the ability to rethink processes, without which technological investment may fail to generate lasting value.
3.4.3.
The EESC draws attention to the specific difficulties encountered by micro-enterprises and SMEs, which form the backbone of the EU economy. These businesses face significant barriers linked to the high regulatory burden, the technical complexity of the solutions available and the fragmentation of the single market. Without adequate accompanying measures, there is a risk that the adoption of AI and AM will accentuate the asymmetries between large enterprises and SMEs ( 28 ) .
B.
The role of social dialogue, collective bargaining and worker involvement
3.4.4.
Social dialogue, collective bargaining and the involvement of workers’ representatives at different appropriate levels play a pivotal role in ensuring the economic sustainability and social acceptability of technological innovation and contribute to a human-centred approach and to guaranteeing that workers have an effective voice capable of influencing decision-making processes related to the deployment of AI and AM systems.
3.4.5.
Social dialogue and collective bargaining can be effective tools for facilitating the implementation and the use of AI and AM in the workplace ( 29 ) . They allow general rules to be adapted in a collaborative manner to sectoral and company contexts and strengthen mutual trust between employers and workers, which may lead to wider acceptance of these tools.
3.4.6.
Significant experiences can be observed in various national contexts ( 30 ) . In some countries, legislation recognises the right of workers’ representatives to be informed in detail about the functioning of algorithmic systems that affect work organisation and employment decisions, thereby strengthening transparency and the possibility of preventive intervention. There are also examples of co-determination, such as in Germany, where legislation has been reformed with specific reference to the impact of AI, or systematic consultation, such as in France, where the introduction of AI has already been deemed subject to consultation, including by the courts. In other cases, collective bargaining has introduced figures or committees dedicated to the management of technological innovation, with the task of accompanying the implementation of AI through information, training and structured consultation with workers.
3.4.7.
Furthermore, company agreements ( 31 ) have introduced specific clauses aimed at limiting surveillance and the reuse of data, including a ban on the use of information collected for disciplinary or dismissal purposes and a ban on the use of data for training AI systems for the purpose of replacing human labour. These experiences showcase positive results stemming from effective and informed worker involvement, which can take various forms – from information and consultation to stronger forms of involvement such as co-determination.
3.4.8.
As regards the interplay between the existing EU legislation (the AI Act) and social dialogue, the EESC reiterates its call for the EU AI Office to establish close cooperation with the European cross-sectoral social partners, to ensure that the role of social dialogue is adequately reflected in the AI Office’s upcoming guidelines and in secondary legislation. The EESC further calls on the AI Office to produce clarification regarding all AI systems. In-depth, robust and clearly structured coordination channels between the AI Office and the European Commission’s DG EMPL and DG Connect should be established.
Brussels, 18 March 2026.
The President
of the European Economic and Social Committee
